verses.note: The first mention of public prayer in Scripture stands at the end of a chapter of violence. Calling on the LORD's name is presented as the mark of the line that God preserves, the phrase Joel and Paul use of those who will be saved (Joel 2:32, Romans 10:13).
Abram's life in the land is marked by public worship. Calling on the LORD's name at an altar, where others could see it, declares whose land this is and whose protection he trusts.

The text records no altar and no calling on the LORD's name in Egypt. Its return here, at the same spot as before, suggests that Abram's life with God is being resumed after a lapse. Many interpreters read it as a return in the sense of repentance, though the text does not use that word.

Abram's first recorded words to God are not praise but complaint, and God answers with a fuller promise rather than a rebuke. The lament psalms follow the same pattern: honest speech to God is itself an act of faith.
The text records no prayer from Hagar, only her affliction, and God is said to hear it. Scripture presents suffering itself as something that reaches God, as Israel's groaning does in Exodus 2:23-25.
Abraham's first recorded prayer for another person is for Ishmael. God does not grant it in the form asked, but he hears it (verse 20), and the answer is generous.

Abraham's prayer is an argument from God's own justice. He does not ask God to be less just but to act consistently with his justice, which makes this chapter a model for prayer that appeals to God's character.
Boldness and humility grow together in Abraham's prayer. He dares more precisely because he confesses that he is dust, and God does not rebuke him for it.

God grants every request Abraham makes. The limit of the conversation is set by Abraham's asking, not by God's willingness, which is why many readers take the chapter as an invitation to pray for more than one dares.
Lot's plea echoes Abraham's intercession in form, with its polite formulas and its bargaining, but its subject is only himself. The contrast shows what chapter 18 is about: Abraham asked for others.
Abraham never asked for Lot by name, and ten righteous men were not found. God still answered the heart of the prayer, that the righteous not be swept away with the wicked.

The first mention of prayer with this verb is intercession: one person asking God on behalf of another. It is a prophet's work, and the pattern continues through Moses (Numbers 21:7), Samuel (1 Samuel 12:23), and Job (Job 42:8).

The prayer that heals comes from the man who caused the harm. God answers because he appointed Abraham to pray, not because Abraham has earned a hearing, and the result is life for a household outside the covenant.
No prayer is recorded, only a voice, and God hears it. The verse gives the ground for every cry that has no words: God listens where the one crying lies.

The servant's prayer is specific, humble, and grounded in God's commitment to someone else. He asks not for his own sake but for his master's, appealing to God's chesed. Prayer here is an act of dependence in the middle of an ordinary task.
God answers before the request is complete, the pattern Isaiah 65:24 states as promise and Daniel 9:20-23 describes as experience. The answer was already on its way when the servant began to pray.
Thanksgiving follows the answer immediately and is spoken aloud before anyone else. The servant's prayer life has two movements in one scene: asking (verses 12-14) and blessing (verse 27).

The promise of descendants was sworn to Abraham and certain, yet Isaac still prays for it. The verse teaches that God's promises do not make prayer unnecessary; they are what gives prayer its ground, and God's fulfilment arrives through it.

Rebekah brings her confusion straight to God, not only her request. Scripture treats that kind of honest question as a form of seeking God, and she receives an answer that explains her suffering without removing it.
God's word to Isaac is answered with worship before anything else. The order of the verse, altar, then tent, then well, is the order of a life that puts calling on God before securing its own needs.
Jacob's vow is a prayer that asks God to do what God has just said he will do. However mixed Jacob's motives, the form is sound: the promises of God are what a person has to hold God to.

Leah's words move from petition and complaint to praise within four births. Scripture's psalms often make the same movement, and the verse shows praise offered while the underlying sorrow, an unloved marriage, remains.

Rachel's words assume that she has prayed and that God has heard. The narrator reports her interpretation without endorsing her sense of victory over her sister; the verse shows a real prayer answered while the heart that prayed it is still tangled in rivalry.

The narrator says God listened to Leah before anything is said about the mandrakes, which Rachel, not Leah, now holds. The order of the verse puts the child down to God's hearing, not to the plant or the bargain.

"He listened to her" assumes that Rachel had prayed, perhaps for years. Her new prayer for another son is answered in 35:17-18, at the cost of her life, a reminder that answered prayers in Scripture can carry sorrow as well as joy.

Jacob prays by reminding God of what God has said. The same pattern runs through Scripture's great prayers, such as Moses interceding after the golden calf (Exodus 32:13) and David after Nathan's promise (2 Samuel 7:25). Prayer in this form takes hold of God's word and asks him to keep it.
The prayer is honest about fear. Jacob does not dress up his request; he names the danger and asks for rescue. Scripture treats such plain asking as fitting (Psalm 34:4, Philippians 4:6).
Jacob's summary of his twenty years is that God answered him when he was in trouble. The prayer of 32:9-12 was heard, and the first thing the answered man does is lead others to worship.

Jacob does everything he can (gifts, double silver, the brother) and then prays for what he cannot do: that God would change the heart of a foreign ruler. His prayer is answered in the very man he fears, whose compassion, rachamim, will grow warm for Benjamin in verse 30.

Jacob does not treat the move as a merely practical decision, though Joseph's invitation and Pharaoh's wagons have already settled it. He brings it to God first, at a place where God had spoken to his father, and God answers that night.

Prayer here interrupts prophecy. Rashi connected the line with Samson, the Danite of verse 17, who at the end cried to God for strength (Judges 16:28); read more broadly, the line is the dying father's own confession that he waits for God to act.

The cry that reaches God is not a polished prayer but groaning under a burden. The verse teaches that God hears the cry of the oppressed even when it has not found words, a conviction the Psalms and Paul both echo (Psalm 34:17; Romans 8:26).
Worship begins before the rescue. The people bow down on hearing that God has seen their affliction, before a single plague has fallen, trusting the promise as though it were already done.

Moses' prayer is a complaint, and Scripture records it without rebuke. The lament psalms pray the same way (Psalm 13:1-2; 44:23-26), holding God to his own promises. God answers Moses not with a reprimand but with a renewed promise in 6:1.

Moses prays God's own words back to him. Having heard that God is forgiving and abounding in loyal love, he asks for exactly that. Scripture's intercession often works this way, appealing to what God has revealed about himself.
David's first words answer God's promise with astonishment, not a claim. Prayer that receives a promise begins by recognizing the gap between the gift and the recipient.

David asks for nothing God has not already said. Praying God's promises back to him is not reminding a forgetful God; it is aligning desire with God's stated purpose, and aiming the answer at God's honor.
Persistent prayer in the face of silence is presented as faithful, not faithless. The psalm does not explain the silence; it keeps praying through it.
The plea ‘be not far’ occurs three times (verses 1, 11, 19), marking the structure of the lament. Prayer here is the refusal to accept God's distance as final.

The final act of the Servant is intercession for transgressors. Luke records Jesus praying for those crucifying him (Luke 23:34, a verse absent from some early manuscripts), and the New Testament describes the risen Christ as always living to intercede (Romans 8:34, Hebrews 7:25).

In the Greek Bible God says ‘I will sanctify (hagiasō) my great name’. Jesus teaches his disciples to pray ‘hallowed (hagiasthētō) be your name’ (Matthew 6:9), a prayer that God do what Ezekiel promised. The Jewish Kaddish, which opens by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified, takes its wording from the similar promise in Ezekiel 38:23.

Restoration includes the restoration of prayer. A God who had said ‘I will not be consulted’ now invites Israel to ask, and promises to answer. The New Testament's confidence that believers may approach God boldly (Hebrews 4:16) rests on the same reopened access.

The promise of restoration drives Daniel to prayer rather than replacing it. Biblical prayer does not treat God's sovereign plan as a reason to stop asking; it asks for what God has promised, on the ground that he has promised it.
The model prayer ends not in calm resignation but in urgency: forgive, act, do not delay. Humility before God and boldness toward God belong together here.
The answer is dispatched at the beginning of the prayer, before the confession is complete. God's response is not earned by the length or eloquence of the prayer, yet it comes to the one who prays.
Prayer is speech addressed to God, and the verse exposes prayer that is really addressed to the onlookers. The warning applies to any setting where praying well earns a reputation.

If the Father already knows what his children need, prayer is not information or persuasion but the trust of children speaking to a father. The verse removes the reason for anxious repetition without removing the command to ask, which 7:7-11 will press.
The prayer teaches the order of desire: God's glory first, then human need. The plural ‘our’ makes every disciple's private prayer an act of the whole family of God.
The prayer ends with an admission of weakness. Disciples who have asked for God's kingdom still need to be kept from falling, and they say so.

Prayer is described as asking, seeking, and knocking, and each is promised an answer. The promise does not guarantee the thing asked for in the form asked; verses 9 to 11 will show that the Father gives what is good.
Prayer rests on the character of the one addressed. The argument does not claim that asking earns anything; it claims that the Father is better than the best human parent.
‘Lord, save us’ became one of the church's shortest prayers. Matthew shapes the disciples' cry as a prayer addressed to Jesus as Lord, which is how Psalm 107 addresses the LORD in the same danger.

Jesus commands prayer for a specific need, workers for the harvest. The verse teaches that God's purposes are carried out through the prayers of his people, and that those who pray are often the answer to their own request.

After the crowds and before the storm, Jesus prays alone. Matthew shows him praying on a mountain here and in Gethsemane (26:36-44), both times at night and both times while his disciples face a trial they do not yet understand. The disciples struggle on the water while he prays for them, a pattern the church has long seen in Christ's continuing intercession (Hebrews 7:25).

Her prayer is three words in Greek, the cry of the psalmist, “Help me, O LORD my God” (Psalm 109:26). It asks for nothing she can claim but mercy, and it keeps asking. The father of the convulsed boy will pray the same verb, ‘help my unbelief’ (Mark 9:24).

Before he breaks the bread Jesus gives thanks, as Jewish custom did at every meal. Paul later tells Timothy that everything God created is good and received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4-5), and he himself gave thanks before eating on the storm-tossed ship (Acts 27:35).

Mark shows Jesus praying at three moments, each at night and each at a turning point: here after his first success, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32-39). Prayer comes before decisions about what to do next.

After his greatest public miracle, when the crowd would have made him king, Jesus goes alone to pray. The verse shows prayer as the place where Jesus' mission is kept on the Father's course rather than the crowd's.
The disciples' power had come from Jesus, and it did not become theirs to use apart from him. Prayer here is the posture of dependence on God that keeps authority from turning into technique.

Jesus teaches bold and expectant prayer that rests on God's goodness and power. The New Testament qualifies this promise by God's will (1 John 5:14) and shows Jesus himself praying ‘not what I will’ (14:36), so the verse is an invitation to trust, not a technique for obtaining what one wants.

Forgiving others is bound up with receiving God's forgiveness. Jesus does not make human forgiveness the price of God's, but he makes the unforgiving heart incompatible with the prayer that asks mercy for itself.
Even within God's plan for history, Jesus tells his disciples to pray about the conditions of their suffering. Prayer is not resignation to what must happen; it asks for mercy within it.

The prayer joins complete trust (Abba, all things are possible for you), honest request (take this cup), and surrender (not what I will). It gives the church permission to ask God plainly for what it wants while submitting to what he wills.
Jesus prays the same prayer twice, then a third time (Matthew 26:44). Returning to the same request in anguish is part of faithful prayer, as Paul's threefold plea in 2 Corinthians 12:8 also shows.

The scene joins the priest's incense with the people's prayers, the connection Psalm 141:2 makes and Revelation 8:3-4 pictures in heaven. Luke's first scene of revelation takes place during prayer, a pattern he repeats at Jesus' baptism (3:21) and transfiguration (9:29).
A prayer Zechariah had likely given up on is heard. The verse shows that the delay of an answer is not its refusal, and the answer, when it comes, is larger than the request.
Anna's worship is night and day, with fasting and prayer. Luke later commends persistent prayer through a widow who will not stop asking (18:1-8).
Heaven opens while Jesus prays. Luke presents the Son's life as lived in communion with the Father, and the decisive revelations of his identity come in prayer (9:28-35).

Luke more than any Gospel shows Jesus praying at turning points (3:21, 6:12, 9:18, 9:28-29, 22:41). Here prayer is a regular rhythm set against popularity: the more the crowds come, the more he withdraws.

Luke shows Jesus praying before decisive acts: at the baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28-29), and on the Mount of Olives (22:41-44). The church in Acts follows the pattern, praying before choosing Matthias and before sending Barnabas and Saul (Acts 1:24, 13:2-3).

Luke sets the turning points of Jesus' ministry in prayer: his baptism (3:21), the choosing of the Twelve (6:12), this confession, the transfiguration (9:28-29), the Lord's Prayer (11:1), and Gethsemane (22:41-44). Revelation about who Jesus is comes in the setting of his communion with the Father.
The transfiguration happens while Jesus prays (verse 29). In Luke the revelation of Jesus' glory is not a stage effect for the disciples but the outward showing of his communion with the Father.
Mission begins as petition. The disciples are told to ask the Lord of the harvest for laborers, and in the next breath Jesus sends them, so those who pray become the answer to their own request.

The disciples learn to pray by watching Jesus pray. Prayer in Luke is first the Son's own practice (3:21, 6:12, 9:18, 9:28) and only then something he teaches, so Christian prayer is a sharing in his relation to the Father.
The first concern of prayer is God's name and God's reign. Before asking for anything for themselves, disciples ask God to be honored and to rule, which reorders every request that follows.

Asking God for ordinary needs is not beneath prayer. The petition for bread sits directly under the petitions for God's name and kingdom, joining the largest hopes and the smallest needs in a single prayer.

The final petition asks God for protection in the time of trial, the same prayer Jesus urges on the disciples in Gethsemane (22:40, 46). Luke's Jesus has faced such testing himself (4:1-13), and he commends the disciples who stood by him in his trials (22:28).

The story's setting makes the point before its conclusion does: in a culture of hospitality, no neighbor refuses bread for a guest. If an ordinary neighbor at midnight will help, prayer to God cannot be less sure.
Whatever the word means, the argument runs from the lesser to the greater. God is not the grudging neighbor; he is the Father of verse 13, and boldness in asking is fitting for those who know him.

Jesus commands persistent asking and promises an answer. Verse 13 defines the best of what is given, and Jesus' own prayer in Gethsemane (22:42) shows that asking includes yielding to the Father's will; together they keep the promise from becoming a formula for getting what one names.
Knowing that the Father already knows does not make prayer for bread pointless (11:3). It changes its tone, from anxious pleading to trusting request.

The verse makes persistence the mark of Christian prayer and names its enemy: not unbelief first, but weariness. Prayer ‘at all times’ is set within the long wait for the Son of Man, so it is the ordinary breath of a people who hope.

The verse grounds persistent prayer not in overcoming God's reluctance but in his character and his choice of his people. The cry ‘day and night’ is heard by one who is already committed to the ones crying.

Thanksgiving is right and commanded; the Pharisee's fault is that his thanks become a report of his own merits and a verdict on another worshiper. The verse shows prayer that addresses God while measuring oneself against people.
The blind man's cry is the parable of verses 1-8 lived out: he will not be silenced, and he is heard. His words, joined to the tax collector's, stand behind the Jesus Prayer of Eastern Christianity.

Prayer is the means of watchfulness. Jesus does not ask disciples to hold themselves ready by effort alone but to ask for strength, and in Gethsemane he will pray while they sleep, teaching by example what he commands here (22:41-46).

Jesus' prayer comes before Peter's fall, and it does not ask that Peter be spared the sifting but that his faith not fail within it. Christ's intercession is aimed at perseverance through failure, not at the avoidance of every trial (Romans 8:34, Hebrews 7:25).

Jesus' first word in the garden is not about his own anguish but about the disciples' danger. Prayer, in his teaching, is the defense against the moment of testing, and the phrase ties the command directly to the petition he gave them in 11:4.

The prayer joins honest request and complete surrender without cancelling either. Jesus asks for what he wants, and he wants the Father's will more. It is the Lord's Prayer ‘Your will be done’ prayed at the point of greatest cost.

Luke's frame makes the garden scene a lesson as well as a record. Jesus meets his hour by praying and enters it strengthened; the disciples sleep and enter it unready, and within minutes they reach for swords and scatter.

All three of Jesus' prayers in Luke's passion begin with ‘Father’ (22:42, 23:34, 23:46). The Son who first spoke of ‘My Father's house’ as a boy (2:49) dies with the same trust, and he dies praying Scripture.

The sisters pray by describing their need and naming Jesus' love, without telling him what to do. The rest of the chapter shows that such prayer is heard, though not answered on the petitioner's schedule.
Martha believes that Jesus' prayers are heard by God, a belief the chapter confirms (verses 41-42). Her faith is real and incomplete at the same time, and Jesus meets it where it is.

Jesus' prayer is thanksgiving grounded in unbroken communion with the Father, not an appeal for power he lacks. Elijah before the fire at Carmel also prayed aloud so that the people would know the LORD was God (1 Kings 18:36-37); Jesus prays so they will know the Father sent him.

The earliest Christians prayed to Jesus as well as through him: Stephen commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus (Acts 7:59) and Paul addresses those who call on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:2). Verse 14, with its ‘ask me’, belongs to that practice. Because the goal is the Father's glory in the Son, the promise is not a formula that secures any request, but an invitation to ask for what serves his purposes.

The promise is given to those in whom Jesus' words remain, so that their wishes have been shaped by his words. Prayer here is not a way of bending God to the disciple's will but the asking of those whose will is being formed by the word of Christ.

After Easter the disciples stand before the Father in the Son's name, with the access that belongs to him. The promise does not bypass Jesus; it is because they come in his name that they may ask the Father directly.

The goal of prayer in Jesus' name is joy, and joy in its fullness. The Synoptic promise, ask and it will be given you (Matthew 7:7), is here tied to the new access the disciples will have after the resurrection.

Jesus' intercession is not the persuasion of an unwilling Father. The Father already loves those who love his Son; the Son's intercession and the Father's love are one will for their good, and prayer in his name is the privilege of children, not the petition of strangers.

Jesus' prayer for his disciples is also a gift to them: hearing him pray for them is part of how his joy becomes theirs. The church has continued to find strength in overhearing this prayer, which is why it has been read at ordinations, at the Lord's Supper, and at gatherings for Christian unity.
Prayer is not an addition to the church's life but one of its four foundations, continuing the prayer that preceded Pentecost (1:14).
Paul's prayer is ceaseless, specific, and submitted to God's will. His thanks are offered ‘through Jesus Christ’: even gratitude reaches God through the mediator.
Christian prayer is the cry of adopted children, prompted by the Spirit and using the Son's own word for the Father. The Spirit does not replace the believer's prayer; he makes it possible.
The verse is a comfort to anyone who cannot find words to pray. Weakness in prayer is expected, and the Spirit intercedes where believers' understanding fails.
Prayer that cannot be put into words is still known and answered by God. The Spirit's intercession always matches the will of God, which believers' own prayers do not.
Paul's teaching turns to prayer, and his prayer is shaped by his teaching. He prays not for circumstances but that believers would understand what they already have in Christ.

Paul's first request for the church is not for circumstances but for knowledge of God's will leading to a worthy life. The prayer is a pattern for intercession, asking for character and understanding before comfort.
Prayer is described as priestly approach to God's throne, open to every believer because of Christ's priesthood. It is marked by confidence, not presumption, because the throne is one of grace.

Jesus' prayer was real struggle, voiced aloud and with tears, and the verse calls it ‘heard’. It gives the church a model of prayer that is honest about fear and yet yielded to God, and it grounds the invitation of 4:16 to approach the throne of grace in time of need.
Because Christ now appears before God on our behalf, believers pray as those represented at the throne. His presence there grounds the confidence of 4:16 and the intercession of 7:25.
